Finally, we discuss the potential risks and limitations of using data-driven modeling techniques in the context of social systems. The proliferation of botnets has become a major concern in the cybersecurity landscape
due to their effectiveness in launching DDoS attacks on targets with substantial IP
infrastructure. Identifying the source IP addresses of botnet operations is crucial for
mitigating these threats, as it enables targeted protection. Our research leverages
natural language processing techniques to analyze command logs generated by
honeypot servers, leading to a novel approach for identifying botnet attack clusters
through IP address groups. Our analysis of DDoS command logs from honeypot servers
yielded a finding that IP clusters can be distinguished by their command patterns,
enabling the development of a predictive model that accurately forecasts IP clusters
associated with botnet attacks. Our model achieved a remarkable 97.3% accuracy in
simulated testing. Moreover, when applied to real-world honeypot command logs, it
successfully detected IP clusters associated with DDoS attacks on servers running
Nginx, yielding an impressive 97.1% accuracy in validation tests. Our findings
demonstrate the efficacy of using machine learning and text analysis to identify
botnet attack clusters, paving the way for real-time detection of such attacks. Our
research has been accepted for presentation at the 2022 International Conference
on Artificial Intelligence Technologies for System Analytics (ICTSA 2022). The
authors are available for collaboration on further developments. The accompanying
source code and documentation are available at the associated GitHub repository.

Our findings reveal that these value-iteration algorithms result in regret that diminishes at a rate proportional to $n^{1/2+\epsilon}$, where $\epsilon$ is a small positive value, for any $\epsilon>0$. Furthermore, we establish that this regret rate is both a threshold for performance assessment of value-iteration algorithms and an optimal rate for achieving first-order critical points in offline reinforcement learning problems. Alongside this, we also design a new value-iteration algorithm that attains the optimal rate for achieving first-order critical points with a regret rate that diminishes at a rate proportional to $n^{-3/10}$, which represents the currently fastest known rate in such contexts. Our analysis is founded upon two key theoretical frameworks: a novel approach to addressing offline reinforcement learning problems using a two-stage optimization strategy involving a lower bound of the objective function and a higher bound of the optimal solution, and a novel application of the Weierstrass theorem in the study of the critical points of offline reinforcement learning problems. Additionally, we provide empirical evidence to validate the practical efficacy of our value-iteration algorithms in addressing various offline reinforcement learning problems. A deep learning approach for brain tumor image segmentation (BTS) is becoming a highly sought-after solution due to the inherent difficulties in this task. Traditional deep learning methods for BTS often neglect contextual information, which is crucial for accurate segmentation. To address this limitation, we propose a novel 3D convolutional neural network, which integrates contextual information at multiple scales. Our network, which combines a 3D U-Net with 3D atrous convolutional layers, achieves this goal by using skip connections to combine feature maps. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach on a publicly available dataset for brain tumor segmentation. Our results demonstrate that the proposed 3D U-Net architecture outperforms a standard 3D U-Net in terms of segmentation accuracy, achieving a higher Dice coefficient. Moreover, we observe that the contextual information provided by the additional features improves the overall segmentation quality. Notably, the proposed network also exhibits a high level of precision, as indicated by a low Hausdorff distance. We introduce a novel technique to categorize models based on their component relationships using tree-like structures. Our method involves creating a unique representation of each component model that enables efficient analysis of combined systems. We demonstrate that this approach allows for the direct synthesis of models representing the entire system from the individual component models, without needing to compute the combined model explicitly. We demonstrate that our method facilitates more efficient parallelization in model checking for complex systems with interconnected Markov chains, significantly reducing the time required for processing large models. Furthermore, we show that our approach enables the parallelization of model checking for POMDPs by representing uncertain states as hidden variables and applying our technique to Markov decision processes. Locating specific visual items in paperwork is a common and efficient method for extracting information from historical images. In this study, a novel approach to finding shapes within a document is presented, utilizing a pre-trained neural network to identify clusters of shapes and then using a combination of clustering techniques and shape analysis to locate individual items. Additionally, this method allows for the prediction of whether shapes are interconnected, which can be particularly useful for identifying groupings within a document. Experimental results demonstrate that our method performs comparably to other leading techniques when detecting individual shapes, yet produces more accurate groupings due to its ability to accurately identify interconnected shapes. A publicly accessible dataset containing a large collection of shape groupings from document images is also provided for further research. The source code for our method is available on GitHub under the document-detectors repository. https://github.com/ekantchouline/document-detectors/tree/master/graphical-object-detectors/python.

Initially, we revisit the fundamental concepts underlying Pontryagin's Minimum Principle and introduce a simplified example demonstrating its application. We then examine the development and analysis of the necessary conditions for an optimal solution within linear quadratic and non-linear quadratic optimal control problems. Subsequently, we delve into the topic of contemporary state-constrained and feedback control strategies, encompassing recent advancements in low-dimensional convex optimization techniques. We also explore the concept of embedded optimization within optimal control theory. Furthermore, we explore the field of non-linear programming and optimization techniques, including gradient and Newton's methods, as well as alternative approaches leveraging problem-specific structures and relaxation methods. Finally, we highlight the key challenges and emerging trends in the field of optimal control law synthesis. This paper introduces a novel approach to tackle the computational and memory constraints associated with end-to-end temporal video modelling by adopting a memory-efficient strategy that divides a long video into multiple short segments. A key contribution of this method is a technique called gradient forward-propagation, which enables efficient propagation of gradients and avoidance of data duplication, thereby significantly reducing memory consumption. Moreover, the approach can be seamlessly integrated with various RNN architectures, including LSTM and GRU, and its effectiveness has been demonstrated through its high performance on two prominent video classification tasks - Kinetics and Something-Something. Notably, the approach can handle large-scale temporal modelling with significantly reduced memory usage, making it a highly efficient solution. Code for the approach is available on GitHub. Our experiments show that this method can achieve comparable results to existing top-performing models, but with a substantial reduction in memory usage. Specifically, the approach can handle 4K temporal inputs with a memory footprint of less than 8GB on an A100 GPU, whereas prior models required 32-64GB. Our findings suggest that this method has the potential to unlock new possibilities for end-to-end temporal modelling. The rise of the pre-trained model (PTM) era has significantly increased the value of large datasets, prompting dataset owners to implement effective copyright protection methods. However, existing methods are vulnerable to attacks that can potentially compromise copyright ownership. In response, this study proposes a new concept of harmless and stealthy copyright protection through the use of untargeted backdoor watermarks. Unlike previous approaches, this method incorporates a designed backdoor trigger that does not adversely affect model performance. Through extensive experiments, the proposed method has been shown to surpass existing methods in terms of both the success rate of dataset ownership verification and model accuracy preservation. Notably, it has also demonstrated resilience against various types of attacks. Moreover, the study presents a theoretical analysis of the trade-off between the robustness of the proposed method and its susceptibility to attacks. This analysis provides insights into the relationship between misclassification rate and attack success rate. Ultimately, the study provides a comprehensive solution for the challenging task of both strong watermarking and strong data protection. This manuscript focuses on the potential of the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) to uncover new insights into the fundamental forces of quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at its limits of applicability. The EIC's unique combination of high-momentum transfer and high-energy collisions enables it to probe the intricate interplay between gluon density, parton showering, and hadronic medium formation. Theoretical frameworks, including QCD factorization and parton showers, are thoroughly evaluated in the context of jet and jet substructure studies. The utility of the EIC precision QCD for refining global parton distribution function (PDF) analyses and for informing the development of the future precision QCD (FPQCD) program at the United States Particle Accelerator Laboratory (Argonne) are also explored. The efficacy of our approach was experimentally validated in two applications: predicting future activities and detecting changes in activity patterns over time. The results indicate that our model outperforms the baseline in both tasks, with results showing a high degree of agreement. We extend the constructive approach in cryptography to account for interactive protocols, enabling a fresh perspective on information flow analysis and the exploration of new concepts. Specifically, we develop a formal language for interactive constructive security proofs, which are re-evaluated as sequences of security protocols. This language facilitates the demonstration of a crucial property called 'interactivity,' where a pair of protocols supporting a constructive proof also provide individual security guarantees.

These findings represent a pioneering effort in applying the constructive approach to interactive protocols, offering novel insights and security proofs within this domain.

This paper introduces a novel approach that utilizes a bi-directional model comparison method for loop detection, which we combine with a Visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (VSLAM) method to enable robust navigation and map creation in real-time. Our method leverages the entire sequence of images to derive a global pose graph, which we then match against a pre-generated map of local keyframe images. Subsequently, we utilize the information from the matched keyframe images to generate a short-term trajectory, which we then integrate into the overall pose graph to determine the current pose. We evaluate the performance of our method on various datasets, achieving a 95.76% accuracy in identifying loop closures and demonstrating a 5 cm root mean square detection error in real-world experiments. Deep neural networks are vulnerable to manipulation by malicious individuals who can deceive them with carefully crafted images or text. A common strategy for strengthening these models against these threats is known as adversarial training, where the defenses are strengthened by exposing them to simulated attacks. However, conventional methods that use a 'black box' approach to model performance lacks clear indicators of the model's resilience, making it difficult to identify the source of each attack. In this study, a new training method called Latent Boundary-guided Adversarial Training (LADDER) is proposed, which enhances the defenses by incorporating the boundaries of the latent space where images shift when under attack. LADDER's approach is unique in that it incorporates multiple types of boundaries to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the semantics of the input data. Through a combination of theoretical and empirical analysis, it is shown that LADDER's boundaries are distinct from those of standard models and provide a more effective defense against various types of attacks. Furthermore, LADDER's design allows it to be easily adapted to different types of attacks and to improve the performance of other defense methods. When applied to a variety of image and text datasets, LADDER outperformed existing methods in both theoretical and practical evaluations, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing the resilience of deep neural networks against malicious attacks. The code for LADDER is available for public review at https://github.com/THUMLD/LADDER. A custom sensor design featuring a 3.5 mm pupil size and 1280 lines per degree can detect minute wavefront distortions with an expected sensitivity of 0.3 $\mu$m (rms) at 700 nm. Initial sensor prototypes have been developed and tested to validate performance, with encouraging results indicating that the upgrade will yield near-optimal AO system performance according to the original specifications. Bird classification in computer vision has significant applications such as wildlife monitoring and environmental research. Traditional deep learning methods require extensive annotated datasets, which is a major challenge in bird species classification due to the time and effort involved. This research presents a novel approach utilizing transfer learning to improve classification accuracy with a reduced amount of data. It proposes a multi-stage training technique that enables the model to learn from multiple datasets, resulting in a better understanding of various bird species. Furthermore, we suggest a method to leverage expert knowledge, such as bird classification reports, to automate the process of creating labels. This paper presents a comprehensive case study of the implementation of this approach, utilizing a dataset of 15 bird species, along with the evaluation of its effectiveness using multiple metrics. The results demonstrate that this approach achieves an impressive accuracy rate of 98.75% in a multi-class classification task, outperforming the original model by 7.5%. Additionally, it reduces the training time by 3 times and the number of required labels by 4 times. The approach also shows its ability to adapt to new data by achieving an accuracy rate of 94.7% in a semi-supervised task, using only 13% of the original dataset. Overall, this work presents a significant contribution to the field of bird species classification. It is the first to utilize transfer learning with a multi-stage training technique in this domain, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods in various evaluation metrics. Cache side-channel attacks can extract confidential data from the cache of a target CPU, and these attacks can cause significant security breaches in software. However, the cache side-channel threat is difficult to assess due to the vast number of possible program inputs, making it challenging to track cache hits and misses. In this study, we introduce CacheQL, a tool that identifies cache side-channel vulnerabilities in large applications. CacheQL uses a combination of static and dynamic analysis to map the program's memory and identify the cache lines affected by the target function. It then uses these cache lines to create a precise trigger model to locate the cache side-channel vulnerability. CacheQL's effectiveness was tested on various applications and third-party libraries, and the results show its ability to accurately detect cache side-channel vulnerabilities in large software. Notably, CacheQL identified 8 previously unknown vulnerabilities in popular libraries, including curl, and one in the Linux kernel, and successfully validated the cache side-channel attacks reported in recent research. Additionally, CacheQL's high precision was confirmed by manually verifying the cache line mappings it produced. CacheQL's source code is freely available on GitHub. https://github.com/bk0ptimizer/CacheQL.git. Further information about the study can be found at https://sites.google.com/view/cacheql. This research focuses on a bearing-based formation tracking problem for a group of non-holonomic robots. Building upon a previous study that introduced a centralized controller for this issue, the current work aims to develop decentralized control strategies. The first design utilizes a proportional-differential controller, while the second leverages a proportional-integral controller. To demonstrate the effectiveness of these control strategies, the trajectory tracking problem is reformulated as an optimal problem, and the resulting Sliding Mode Control laws are presented. Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have gained widespread acceptance for their ability to produce high-quality synthetic data in various fields. Despite their capabilities, GAN training poses significant challenges, primarily due to the non-convergence issue. This paper examines the relationship between mode collapse, which is a common problem in GAN training. Mode collapse occurs when a GAN fails to generate multiple distinct samples during training. To address this challenge, the paper proposes an innovative method to identify and measure mode collapse in GAN training. This method is based on analyzing the Hessian eigenvalues of the energy landscape in the parameter space of the GAN generator. To validate the proposed approach, a range of experiments were conducted using different GAN architectures, including DCGAN, BigGAN, and StyleGAN. The results of these experiments were compared with those of existing mode collapse detection methods in the literature. Furthermore, the analysis revealed the relationship between mode collapse and non-convergence in GAN training. The findings of this study are expected to provide valuable insights for researchers working on GAN training. All the source code, datasets, and experimental datasets used in this study are available on GitHub for further analysis. This research aims to contribute to the ongoing research in GAN training and mode collapse detection. The authors hope that this work will inspire researchers to develop more efficient mode collapse detection methods and GAN training algorithms. The open-source code and datasets used in this study are available at the following repository: https://github.com/AbdulTariqFarrukh/Mode-Collapse-Detection. More information about the experimental datasets used in this study can be found at the following website: https://github.com/ElementInfomatics/Experimental-Datasets. Real-world networks comprising multiple layers are prevalent in social, biological, and technological fields, with each layer representing a distinct relationship, such as co-authorship or user interactions.  The task of link prediction in multi-layer networks aims to identify potential connections between nodes across different layers, which can uncover novel relationships within a network and facilitate applications in recommender systems and disease spread modeling.  Despite its importance, this problem remains unsolved  due to the lack of effective algorithms capable of learning the complex structure of interconnected relationships across multiple network layers.  In this research, we introduce MultiSAGE, a novel algorithm that learns the structure of interconnected relationships across multiple network layers by treating each layer as a separate feature and applying a modified version of the SAGE global model, which effectively aggregates features from all the network layers.  Our experiments on multiple social and biological networks demonstrate that MultiSAGE significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art algorithms in predicting links between nodes across different network layers.  Our findings suggest that the global structure of interconnected relationships across multiple network layers is more critical than the local structure within individual layers for accurate link prediction.  Our work provides a foundation for the development of future algorithms capable of effectively learning the structure of interconnected relationships across multiple network layers. This paper proposes an innovative approach to enumerate the results of join queries with projections in a database, efficiently ranking them according to specified preferences. By utilizing a combination of partitioning and bucketing techniques, the proposed method significantly reduces the processing time associated with ranked counting. Furthermore, this method can be easily integrated into existing database querying systems to facilitate quick and efficient enumeration of query results, thereby enhancing overall query performance. Experimental results demonstrate that this proposed method can achieve a substantial reduction in processing time, thereby improving query performance in comparison to existing methods. The Home Service Assignment, Routing, and Scheduling Problem (HSARS) is a complex challenge faced by companies offering home service delivery, particularly those dealing with highly unpredictable customer schedules and the time required for service.  To address this issue, we have developed a two-stage solution strategy, combining column generation and optimization techniques to tackle the HSARS in an efficient manner.  Specifically, we have integrated a Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) model with a simulated approach to account for the uncertainty related to travel and service times, as well as customer cancellations.  Through rigorous testing using real-world data from a major US city, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of our method in achieving high-quality solutions, with cancellation rates under 10% and service times under 60 minutes for over 90% of assignments.  Notably, the computational results we have obtained are significantly better than those produced by current optimization methods, with a substantial cost reduction of up to 30%.  Furthermore, our approach outperforms existing heuristics by delivering solutions that are nearly 90% as good as the ideal.  To the best of our knowledge, our work represents a pioneering effort in addressing the HSARS problem with a focus on uncertainty.  As a result, our research provides valuable insights and practical tools for service providers seeking to optimize their home service operations in the face of changing customer schedules and service times. This research presents a novel method for 3D object orientation estimation using machine perception, involving a low-power passive radio frequency identification tag with an integrated antenna that reflects a probing signal from an access point with multiple antennas to produce multiple-copy signals with a known time-frequency correlation function. From these signals, the tag's three-dimensional orientation can be accurately determined by designing a coding scheme that encodes the tag's location within a three-dimensional space. Our proposed design, the backscatter array codes (BACs), utilizes a combination of Hadamard and Toeplitz matrices to optimize the tag's performance, and we evaluate its performance under various channel conditions. Additionally, the proposed BACs are compared to existing BACs and orientation estimation methods to demonstrate their improved accuracy. Simulations demonstrate that BACs achieve a 50% reduction in orientation estimation error and a 25% reduction in standard deviation compared to the current state-of-the-art. Moreover, the proposed BACs are shown to be robust against fading channels, and their performance remains within a 5% increase in orientation estimation error. Our proposed BACs are designed to be scalable and adaptable to different antenna configurations, and we plan to implement them on a real-world object, such as a smart toy, to test their performance in a real-world environment. One of the key challenges in ensemble learning is creating a diverse set of individual learners that can effectively work together. Our goal is to develop a combiner that can accurately predict the tasks based on the input, even when individual predictors perform poorly. To achieve this, we introduce a combiner that can enhance the overall performance of the predictors. Our proposed method is based on the idea of task predictability, which measures the accuracy of a predictor for a given task. We develop a model that can predict this task predictability, which we call the joint predictability score. By combining the scores of the individual predictors, we can improve the overall performance of the model. Our experimental results show that this approach can effectively combine predictors and achieve better performance compared to existing methods. Moreover, we demonstrate that this approach can also be used to identify the most relevant tasks for a given input. Our analysis of the results reveals that this can be done by predicting the task with the highest joint score. This concept is essential for protecting privacy but is challenging to implement in models that use end-to-end training methods. AIT is a unique mapping that transforms raw data into a more structured representation, allowing for greater control over a model's learnability. To achieve this control, AIT is trained alongside a model using a dual optimization process. This process involves training a model to perform well on a given task while an adversary is trained to make the model misclassify data from a given set. To evaluate the effectiveness of AIT, a novel metric called learnability leakage is developed. This metric measures the degree to which a model can learn specific features. Experimental results show that AIT can effectively reduce learnability leakage while maintaining a model's overall performance. Furthermore, AIT is found to provide more privacy protection than existing methods, such as differential privacy. This is because AIT does not rely on additional noise or perturbations to control a model's learnability. Instead, it uses a mapping that can be easily controlled to conceal sensitive features. Overall, AIT offers a more practical and efficient way to control a model's learnability compared to existing methods. This adaptive approach is particularly useful in complex settings where objects constantly change appearance, such as when identifying people in public areas. By leveraging a dynamic network architecture that can modify itself in response to input, our system can effectively detect and learn from objects in real-time. This innovative approach has far-reaching implications for the use of neural networks in a range of applications, including autonomous systems and robotics. A new type of multi-dimensional Lie algebra is developed and its associated multi-component non-isospectral KdV hierarchy is introduced. This hierarchy is defined by a matrix Riemann-Hilbert problem with a non-perturbative scattering data. The hierarchy's non-isospectral solution is constructed using the nonlinear Fourier method. Finally, the multi-component non-isospectral soliton solutions of the proposed KdV hierarchies are also presented. The obtained results are expected to provide a new perspective on the field theory of multi-component KdV hierarchies. Transformers activated through sparsity have been a popular choice for enhancing model interpretability and reducing computational requirements. However, current sparse transformers often come with a higher parameter count than their dense counterparts, increasing model size and computational costs. To address this issue, we introduce Gating Dropout (GDR), a versatile regularization technique that enables the use of sparse activation while maintaining a comparable model size to dense transformers. GDR achieves this by selectively dropping input tokens during training, rather than activating them sparsely. Although GDR can be integrated into various sparse transformer architectures, we find that it is particularly compatible with the Transformer-XL model. Our experiments show that GDR enables Transformer-XL to achieve a 40% reduction in model size while maintaining or enhancing its performance across tasks like text translation, summarization, and question answering. Notably, GDR also improves the accuracy of dense Transformer-XL, demonstrating its versatility as a standalone regularizer. Additionally, we observe that GDR can be applied not just to input tokens but also to attention weights, further enhancing model performance. Overall, GDR offers a valuable tool for researchers working on sparse transformers, offering a flexible way to trade off between model size and computational requirements, as well as model accuracy. Current approaches either rely solely on known patterns or propose novel hypotheses without any guidance. These approaches often struggle with high dimensionality, leading to an overwhelming number of possible hypotheses to evaluate, resulting in significant challenges in handling high-dimensional datasets. Furthermore, an enhanced version of PILF, PILF++, incorporates an additional learner to suggest multiple hypotheses, achieving new state-of-the-art performance on both real-world and synthetic datasets. A novel technology called Federated Learning enables the deployment of artificial intelligence models on devices with limited power sources while safeguarding users' personal data. In a vehicular edge computing framework, Federated Learning can be applied to develop predictive models that take into account the unique mobility patterns of individual vehicles. However, the high mobility of connected vehicles in such a framework poses a significant challenge to maintaining data consistency across the fleet. This issue is particularly critical due to the limited power resources of vehicles, which limits their ability to participate in Federated Learning. In this context, we investigate the scenario in which a fleet of connected vehicles synchronizes their learning processes within a limited communication window. To address this challenge, we developed a two-stage optimization approach that minimizes the total communication cost of the fleet by taking into account the limited power resources of the vehicles. This approach involves first determining the optimal number of steps for which local model updates are synchronized and then determining the optimal local loss functions to be used during these synchronization periods. To solve this optimization problem, we developed a novel algorithm that iteratively refines the solutions using a combination of dynamic programming and the alternating direction method of multipliers. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach is efficient and scalable for large-scale fleets consisting of hundreds of vehicles with varying levels of mobility, while significantly reducing the total communication cost by up to 80% compared to existing methods. Moreover, our approach outperforms existing methods in terms of accuracy, achieving a 2% improvement in mean square error when using a larger fleet consisting of 400 vehicles. The corresponding code for this approach is available for download at https://github.com/AmirHsan23/FedLearn-VehMobil. To address this issue, we have developed an innovative method for annotating speech data, leveraging emotional audio stimuli to gather naturalistic emotions expressed through speech. Our approach involves using emotional audio stimuli to elicit authentic emotional responses, thereby generating a substantial amount of annotated data. To demonstrate the potential of this method, we have conducted an experiment involving the analysis of emotional patterns within these stimuli using two distinct analysis techniques. Our findings indicate that emotions expressed through audio stimuli can serve as a valuable resource for emotion classification, providing new insights and perspectives that may not be apparent through traditional analysis methods. The annotated data generated from this experiment will be made publicly available through the SPEAMet project platform. Finally, we have proposed a novel framework for annotating speech data, encompassing the stages of data collection, preprocessing, and analysis. This framework is envisioned as a comprehensive, multi-stage annotation process that can be adapted for various emotion classification applications. To our knowledge, this is the first study to utilize emotional audio stimuli as a means of generating annotated data, thereby expanding the possibilities for emotion classification. A significant vulnerability in machine learning models arises from "adversarial examples," which are crafted to mislead model behavior on specific inputs while appearing normal to humans, posing a particular threat to model trust and reliability. This study delves into the concept of neural backdoors by exploring the feasibility of injecting adversarial perturbations directly into a model's weights, rather than its data, and demonstrates the efficacy of this approach through comprehensive experiments. The results show that introducing adversarial weight perturbations can effectively compromise model accuracy and trigger backdoor attacks with comparable success rates to traditional data-based methods, opening up possibilities for more robust defenses against adversarial techniques. The code and data used in this research can be found on the following repository: https://github.com/ChenglongMaWPI/Adversarial-Weight-Perturbations. This study also presents a new technique for generating adversarial weight perturbations and a method for detecting such backdoors through weight-based signatures. The findings have significant implications for the development of adversarial attacks and defenses in machine learning models. Recent research has shown that certain deep neural networks produce weights that can be represented efficiently by a small number of factors obtained through matrix decomposition. This finding has sparked curiosity about whether similar, lower-dimensional representations of neural network weights could enhance network performance. Building on this concept, we've developed a novel approach to compressing visual neural network weights, specifically addressing the challenge of aligning the compressed weights with their corresponding kernels during training. Our proposed Compressive Weight Alignment (CoWa) method enables the use of compressed weights while maintaining optimal performance. We successfully applied this method to multiple neural networks, achieving significant compression ratios, with minimal impact on performance. For instance, we reduced the number of weight factors in ResNet50 from 1.3 million to 1,500, achieving 99.94% accuracy of the original model. We also explored the interpretability of these compressed weights, identifying the underlying reasons for their effectiveness. Our work provides a foundation for future research into efficient weight compression and efficient neural network performance. programming languages demonstrate the efficacy of our approach in translating programs with

In recent years, Graph Attention Networks (GATs) have become a preferred method for graph representation learning due to their ability to focus on the local neighborhood and capture the essence of graph structure. However, when GATs are applied to real-world problems where side information is available, they can fall short by failing to incorporate this essential information. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach, Mean Field CRF based on GATs (MCGATs), designed to integrate node and edge features in a more comprehensive manner. This proposed model leverages mean-field inference to calculate inference scores, thereby enabling the combination of various node and edge features to produce a final score. Furthermore, to optimize the inference process, we introduce a stochastic gradient descent-based training algorithm. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed model over existing state-of-the-art methods in multiple tasks. Specifically, we achieve notable improvements in tasks such as social network ranking, where our proposed model outperforms the baseline GATs by 10%-20% in terms of Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. Additionally, we observe significant gains in text image embedding tasks, where our proposed model excels by 5%-20% in terms of classification accuracy. In various robotics tasks, particularly those involving complex manipulation, trajectories often consist of high-dimensional paths. This high dimensionality can be a challenge for reinforcement learning models, which need to consider the correlation between consecutive states to make informed decisions. To address this issue, a new RL approach is proposed that encourages policies to produce low-dimensional trajectories by incorporating a penalty function that rewards trajectories with a low Kronecker norm. This norm function is computationally efficient and can be applied to optimize trajectories in the action space rather than the entire state space. By doing so, the approach encourages policies to produce trajectories with low-dimensional paths and can be trained in an end-to-end manner. Furthermore, the approach is designed to be computationally efficient, allowing for training on large datasets within a short time frame. To evaluate its effectiveness, the approach is applied to a complex manipulation task involving a robotic arm and a gripper, where it successfully generates low-dimensional trajectories that are robust to noise. These trajectories are then used to improve the overall performance of the robotic arm. To the authors' knowledge, this is the first work that explicitly encourages low-dimensional trajectories while training a policy in an end-to-end setting. The Forbush decrease is a phenomenon characterized by gradual reduction in galactic cosmic ray counts at Earth, primarily caused by solar wind interactions. To identify these changes, we developed an automated system for detecting Forbush decreases in neutron monitor data and analyzed the underlying solar wind interactions. Our study found that Forbush decreases are associated with variations in solar wind magnetic field strength, solar wind density, and the speed of fast solar wind. Notably, we discovered that Forbush decreases are more closely linked to variations in solar wind density than magnetic field strength. Furthermore, we found that the size of Forbush decreases is influenced by the intensity of the associated magnetic clouds and the speed of the solar wind. Our findings also suggest that Forbush decreases are more pronounced in the October-March period, and exhibit a clear annual variation. To facilitate further research, we have compiled a comprehensive catalog of 150 Forbush decreases, providing a valuable resource for studying solar-terrestrial interactions. Our research provides new insights into the relationship between Forbush decreases and solar wind dynamics, and offers a promising avenue for understanding complex solar wind behavior. Inspired by the fundamental concepts of chip-firing and the triangle-free property, we develop the integral flow chip-firing game for undirected graphs. In this game, an integral flow graph is defined as a graph where the flow at each edge is a whole integer, and an integral flow configuration is a flow distribution that maintains this property. The game is played by repeatedly removing and adding flow units to vertices, adhering to a specific set of rules. The process continues until either a critical vertex reaches a flow value of 0 or a stabilised configuration is reached. Our study reveals that, similar to the fundamental triangular-free property in the standard chip-firing game, the integral flow chip-firing game is characterised by graphs that do not exhibit a specific edge behaviour known as strong integral flow balanceability. We also establish a criterion to determine whether a graph meets this condition. Furthermore, we establish a connection between the standard and integral flow chip-firing games, showing that the standard game can be viewed as a special case of the integral flow game. We also provide a specific set of graph types that exhibit this special case. In addition, we develop a generalisation of this game to include weights on the vertices and edges, leading to the integral flow Markov chain. We also study the behaviour of this chain and determine the conditions under which it is ergodic. We also explore the connections between this chain and the standard Markov chain. Finally, we present a specific set of examples of the generalised game. The results of this paper are supported by computational evidence. The code implementing these findings is publicly available. Furthermore, our model predicts that SARS-CoV-2 variants with increased viral loads and severe symptoms, such as Delta and Alpha variants, are more effective at triggering immune cells, which may explain why these variants cause more severe disease. The model also suggests that targeting the interactions between spike protein and DC-SIGN can help control viral replication and prevent severe disease, which may explain the effectiveness of a specific treatment in clinical trials. Overall, our model provides a more comprehensive understanding of the complex interactions between viral proteins and immune cells, which can help guide the development of effective treatments for SARS-CoV-2. The results of our experiments indicate that this approach is particularly effective against backdoor attacks triggered by physical images, achieving a significant improvement in face recognition accuracy. This study introduces an innovative method for effectively reducing the size of 3D point clouds while maintaining their quality, even when faced with noisy or unreliable data. The approach is based on constructing a hypergraph representation of the point cloud and then employing a matrix inversion to derive a point cloud representation with a reduced number of significant features. The sparsity of the obtained solution naturally filters out noisy or unreliable points, yielding an improved point cloud. Numerical experiments demonstrate the method's efficiency and robustness, surpassing existing state-of-the-art approaches in both point cloud compression and noise filtering. The approach is also shown to be computationally fast, running in nearly linear time. The associated source code is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/taesungkim-clspn/hypergraph_resampling. In NLP applications, many systems struggle with detecting grammatical errors in written English. To address this challenge, we suggest a revised approach. First, we note that not all grammatical mistakes have equal significance and propose developing more effective error detection systems by prioritizing more critical mistakes. To achieve this, we create two distinct datasets, one focusing on more frequent mistakes and the other on more important ones, across both edited and unedited English texts. Our analysis demonstrates that these two types of mistakes are statistically independent and that a model trained on frequent errors does not perform as well as human expectations for more critical errors. However, our research also shows that a model can be improved by incorporating knowledge of the error distribution in a given text. Building on this insight, we develop a two-stage error detection system that first identifies potential mistakes based on frequency, then refines its results using a transformer-based model that utilizes sentence-level error distribution information. The final model's performance is evaluated on both automatic metrics and human assessments, resulting in a test F1 score of 74.5 for edited texts and 68.7 for unedited texts. This paper presents a straightforward and minimal-complexity method for enhancing acoustic scene classification (ASC) using convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Our experiments with the ASC challenge dataset demonstrate that integrating frequency features with basic CNNs yields better results compared to the baseline system. Notably, our approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods with minimal complexity, relying on only three convolutional layers and a fully connected layer. Furthermore, we examine the impact of input feature dimensionality and activation functions on model performance. Our results indicate that employing the sigmoid activation function with a reduced input dimensionality of 64 yields superior ASC performance. Building upon our findings, we introduce two novel models, one utilizing eight frequency bins and the other using 64 bins, both achieving higher accuracy rates compared to existing state-of-the-art methods with reduced complexity. These models yield an average validation accuracy of 0.6385 and 0.6382, respectively, on the ASC challenge dataset. To facilitate further research, we provide the source code for our approach on GitHub at https://github.com/rafaelcarneiro/low-complexity-cnn-acoustic-scene-classification. This includes a detailed examination of their stability and the existence of stable, unstable, and neutrally stable solutions, along with discussions on their asymptotic properties. Additionally, a characterization of QDEs based on their exponentiality is provided, with a specific emphasis on their controllability and observability. The study also demonstrates the applicability of a Pontryagin's maximum principle in the context of QDEs. Ultimately, a range of numerical examples is presented to illustrate the derived QDE-based models. The accompanying appendix features a comprehensive derivation of the fundamental matrix of the homogeneous algebro-differential equation in the context of the quaternion algebra. The study serves as a foundational work in the field of QDEs, with a clear path outlined for future research opportunities. We investigate the concept of nearly optimal support optimality in dynamic hash tables, specifically in terms of space efficiency versus false positives. Our study begins by defining a metric for nearly optimal support optimality and identifying the key challenge of balancing query time and space requirements. To address this issue, we introduce a new variant of dynamic hash functions that leverage a time-varying hash function with a fixed average, achieving a space-time trade-off that is nearly optimal.

Our primary contribution is the Cuckoo Filter, a space-efficient data structure that can handle Boolean operations and has a proven time and space trade-off. In contrast to traditional cuckoo tables, our design eliminates the reliance on hashing collisions being rare, instead using a probabilistic approach to optimize space and query time. Our experimental results demonstrate the practical effectiveness of the Cuckoo Filter in both memory-constrained and general-purpose applications.

To further enhance the Cuckoo Filter's performance, we also propose the Adaptive Cuckoo Filter, which dynamically adjusts the size of the data structure based on predicted query patterns. Our theoretical analysis shows that this adaptive approach achieves a space-time trade-off that is nearly optimal, while empirical evaluations confirm its superiority over other filters, including Cuckoo Filter and Bloom Filter. Ultimately, our experimental results demonstrate that the Adaptive Cuckoo Filter significantly outperforms other filters, offering a promising solution for a wide range of applications. The Cuckoo Filter and its adaptive variant are implemented in C++ and available open-source under the permissive Apache License 2.0. To facilitate reproducibility, the source code and evaluation results are provided on GitHub. a family of Hilbert spaces through a bounded operator network is uniquely

Pretrained multilingual language models, specifically BERT variants, exhibit
exceptional performance in various language understanding tasks across multiple
languages. However, the extent to which these models acquire knowledge
shared across languages, and the methods used to leverage this shared
knowledge, remain poorly understood. Our research investigates how the monolingual
training of BERT models affects their ability to transfer knowledge across
languages, with a specific focus on a downstream task - the Cross-Lingual
Sentiment Analysis. Through a novel approach, combining both fine-tuning and
analysis, we demonstrate that monolingual BERT models possess considerable
cross-lingual capabilities. Specifically, we show that a critical step, aligning
the representations of individual monolingual BERT models, enables the transfer of
knowledge across languages, resulting in significant improvements in task
performance. Our findings indicate that monolingual BERT models can acquire and
transfer substantial cross-lingual knowledge, and that a crucial aspect of this
process involves the alignment of representations across languages, facilitated by
fine-tuning. Our study also reveals that monolingual fine-tuning outperforms a
more complex approach, pretraining a multilingual model, on a downstream task.
Furthermore, we demonstrate that a monolingual BERT model can be effectively
fine-tuned to achieve state-of-the-art performance in sentiment analysis tasks. Overall, our research highlights the
importance of fine-tuning in monolingual BERT models and offers insights into the
mechanisms underlying their cross-lingual capabilities. The code and models used in our study are available at

We introduce a novel, non-local image processing operator derived from a combinatorial optimization problem with a unique, non-convex penalty function. This operator exhibits an unusual, self-balancing behavior, where small fluctuations in input values have the maximal response. Our work demonstrates that this characteristic, combined with a spatial smoothing step, enables the extraction of fine-scale details in input signals. As a result, the proposed non-local operator outperforms conventional approaches like convolution and center-weighted averaging in various applications, including the analysis of texture, image compression, and visual saliency detection. Furthermore, we introduce a new non-local flow model for visual saliency detection, which can be applied in the same framework as convolutional neural networks but without the need for a network optimizer. Our results show that this model produces state-of-the-art performance comparable to that of leading neural network-based methods. We introduce It\^oWave, a generative model for wave synthesis that leverages the It\^o diffusion equation to efficiently synthesize high-quality waveforms. It\^oWave is distinguished by its streamlined architecture, requiring only a single temporal convolution, a single linear transformation, and a single transformation of It\^o standard normal distribution. This reduction in complexity enables It\^oWave to learn the stochastic diffusion process directly from the target waveforms, circumventing the need for intermediate representations like spectrograms. Our experiments demonstrate that It\^oWave produces waveforms with comparable spectral accuracy and significantly reduced artifacts compared to existing stochastic diffusion models, while also facilitating faster training and inference. We further showcase It\^oWave's adaptability to diverse waveforms by synthesizing those with frequencies spanning multiple GHz. Traditional question-answering systems often rely on a single step from question to answer, but humans typically resolve complex queries through a series of logical steps from simpler questions to the final answer. By implementing this innovative approach, we're taking question-answering systems closer to replicating human reasoning and achieving a more transparent, accountable, and trustworthy experience. Recent advancements in optical flow have primarily focused on supervised learning methods using extensive training datasets. In contrast, unsupervised learning methods have garnered less attention despite offering several benefits, including reduced data requirements and improved domain invariance. A new approach, referred to as Multi-Frame Unsupervised RAFT with Full-Image Warping (SMURF), addresses this gap by introducing a novel multi-frame unsupervised learning framework for optical flow estimation. SMURF incorporates a unique multi-frame matching module, a motion-aware warping layer, and a motion-attention module to enable the network to learn from multiple frames and generate high-resolution flow fields. Moreover, SMURF learns to self-supervise its training by calculating the motion cost between different frames and then learning from the relative motion between them. Comprehensive evaluations on benchmark datasets demonstrate that SMURF surpasses state-of-the-art methods in unsupervised learning while achieving comparable performance to supervised methods. Notably, SMURF excels in real-world applications, such as video processing and interpolation, and its code will be made available for further research and development. In this research, we investigate the feasibility of using orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (OFDM) for monostatic radar sensing applications. To achieve this, we develop a comprehensive framework that spans from OFDM radar theory to the derivation of a low-complexity algorithm for phase noise mitigation. The algorithm, known as the reweighted and decoupled alternating direction method of multipliers (RADAM), is designed to estimate radar channel frequency responses. To validate our approach, we conduct a series of experiments in both simulation and real-world scenarios, utilizing data collected by our collaborative partners' unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) in Rome, Italy. The experimental results demonstrate that RADAM can produce accurate frequency estimates with high precision, achieving a root mean square error (RMSE) of approximately 0.05 Hz. Notably, RADAM outperforms existing methods, including the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), the proximal gradient method (PGM), and the standard least squares (LS) estimator. RADAM's effectiveness is also demonstrated in multi-user multi-target sensing applications, where it can achieve a comparable performance to the state-of-the-art methods, while offering a significant reduction in computational complexity. The main contributions of this research are twofold. Firstly, we establish a comprehensive OFDM radar sensing framework that encompasses channel estimation, multi-target sensing, and signal processing. Secondly, we introduce a low-complexity algorithm for phase noise mitigation, which can be applied to various radar sensing scenarios. This research serves as a catalyst for further investigations into the application of OFDM in radar sensing and communication systems. Furthermore, our research explores the implications of this approach on the detection of anomalies in meter data. Our study provides valuable insights into the design of priority rules that balance the recovery of lost data with the need for timely detection of network anomalies. Ultimately, our research contributes to the development of more resilient priority policies that can effectively manage the trade-offs between network reliability and anomaly detection. Our findings suggest that a more adaptive approach to managing packet transmission can lead to improved network reliability and anomaly detection in software-defined smart meter networks. In the context of supervised learning, active learning (AL) is a common strategy used to select unlabeled data samples that maximize the performance of the model, thereby minimizing the need for labeled data. However, current AL methods often prioritize improving model performance during training, but not necessarily on unseen test data. Our research introduces a novel approach, referred to as the "Improving Test performance via active learning" (ITAL) framework, which is designed to enhance test data performance concurrently with active sampling. ITAL achieves this by maintaining separate models for both labeled and unlabeled data, and utilizing the unlabeled model to identify high-risk samples that, when labeled and used for model improvement, result in superior test data performance. Our theoretical analysis confirms the connection between AL performance and test data performance, and we have validated the ITAL framework's effectiveness through experiments on diverse datasets, demonstrating its potential to improve test data performance by up to 9.2\%. Furthermore, our ITAL approach is highly adaptable and can be integrated with existing AL methods to further enhance their capabilities. Our code will be made publicly available. It is worth noting that our ITAL framework is the first to address the issue of simultaneously improving both training and test data performance through active sampling. This research introduces a novel local permutation test for examining conditional independence, with an emphasis on its computational efficiency. Unlike conventional permutation tests, the required statistics do not need to be recalculated for each random permutation, resulting in substantial computational savings. In response, we develop a comprehensive simulation study and comparative analysis to evaluate its performance, specifically comparing the local permutation test with state-of-the-art permutation and non-permutation-based approaches. The results demonstrate that the local permutation test achieves competitive levels of power and accuracy while maintaining efficiency, in some cases surpassing even centralized non-permutation-based tests. In addition, our framework is applicable to various types of independence tests, including conditional dependence assessments, thus offering significant computational benefits. In a demonstration of its practical application, we apply the local permutation test to real-world data from the UK's National Health Service to investigate the relationship between ethnicity and treatment outcomes for diabetic patients. The findings suggest a statistically significant association, with the estimated odds ratio indicating a substantial relationship between ethnicity and treatment outcomes. However, the methods used to train these models rely heavily on optimization processes that may drive the agents to pursue objectives different from their programmed reward specifications, resulting in undesirable behavior. In this research, we aim to investigate and quantify the effects of reward misspecification on real-world systems. We focus specifically on three types of misspecification: reward scaling, reward manipulation, and reward sampling, and propose a framework to detect these issues. Furthermore, we explore ways to mitigate misspecification by developing methods to detect and sample rewards in a way that aligns with desired objectives. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of these methods in mitigating misspecification and ensuring safe and aligned behavior in agents. Our research contributes to the ongoing discussion on reward misspecification and provides tools for detecting and mitigating its effects. We also hope that our findings will inspire researchers to develop new methods to ensure safe and aligned agents. We introduce an efficient method for constructing AMG interpolation operators through reinforcement learning, specifically focusing on the construction of local stencils for the interpolation operator. By formulating the stencil construction as a sequence of decisions driven by rewards, the algorithm iteratively selects the most suitable entries for the stencil, with the ultimate objective of creating an effective intergrid operator. To guide this decision-making process, the algorithm leverages an intermediate multigrid approximation to assess potential stencils, with the aim of accelerating convergence. Moreover, the algorithm incorporates a strategy to dynamically adjust the rewards, thereby preventing the repetitive selection of certain stencil entries. Experimental results on a range of numerical examples, including the Convection-Diffusion equation, reveal that the developed method effectively navigates the vast search space and yields high-quality interpolation operators, resulting in accelerated multigrid convergence. Comparative studies demonstrate the efficacy of the developed method in achieving faster convergence compared to established algorithms such as direct solvers, greedy search, and other state-of-the-art algorithms for stencil construction. Neural networks have successfully addressed numerous complex problems, yet they often fall short in real-world applications due to limitations in resources, particularly memory capacity. This problem becomes even more pronounced in systems that handle a large volume of data, where maintaining large pre-trained neural networks is not feasible. Brain region connectivity can be mapped using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures the interconnectedness of brain voxels.  Traditional fMRI connectivity mapping relies on lower-level measurements, but this approach has limitations, including a lack of precision and bias. This suggests that the semantic differences have a greater impact in the medical domain. One of the primary challenges in the Multiple Imputation by Chained Equations (MICE) procedure is managing multiple variables. A common approach involves categorizing variables into groups based on their number of categories and imputing them one group at a time in a sequential order. However, this strategy has its limitations as it fails to account for the correlations between variables. A more effective alternative is to determine the correlation level between variables and impute variables simultaneously without restricting them to predefined groups. Although this method can be computationally expensive, it may lead to better results. A new strategy is proposed that calculates correlation levels for each variable and selects variables to impute based on these levels. A comparison of this approach with the original MICE method is conducted using a simulation study. Results show that the new strategy performs better than the original method, particularly when dealing with a large number of variables. A modified version of the MICE procedure that incorporates principal component regression is also tested, showing improved performance compared to the original MICE procedure. The impact of the number of imputations on the quality of the imputed data is examined, and it is found that the number of imputations has a greater effect when dealing with a large number of variables. A comparison of imputation methods reveals that the new MICE procedure performs better than other imputation methods, including fully conditional imputation and multivariate imputation by chained equations. In conclusion, this study shows that the new MICE procedure can lead to better results, and its suitability for real-world applications should be further investigated. The discovery of MASCARA-1 b, a hot Jupiter orbiting a relatively cool A-type star, marked an important breakthrough in the field of exoplanet research. This massive gas giant was initially identified through ground-based photometric surveys and later confirmed through high-resolution spectroscopy. Subsequent observations by the Spitzer space telescope revealed that MASCARA-1 b's orbit is nearly polar, and the CHEOPS space telescope found that it experiences daily temperature fluctuations across its visible surface. Our reanalysis of MASCARA-1 b's data using a sophisticated method called Gaussian process regression has led us to believe that it is either a near-polar or polar-orbiting planet. This conclusion is supported by observations from Spitzer and CHEOPS, which together suggest that MASCARA-1 b's orbit is approximately 89.1 degrees, making it one of only a few exoplanets with such an orbit that have been directly observed. Furthermore, the CHEOPS data reveal a daily temperature variation on MASCARA-1 b's visible surface that is consistent with a moderate level of cloud cover. The results show that BinGo successfully identifies 39 of these bugs, including 12 additional bugs not previously reported. Our analysis also includes a comparison with existing tools, including SUGAR and a Go mutation testing tool. The results demonstrate that BinGo outperforms SUGAR in identifying concurrency bugs and surpasses the mutation testing tool in terms of efficiency. Our analysis also includes a case study of real-world Go applications, where BinGo identifies multiple bugs, including a critical one affecting a popular Go application. In this study, we investigate a class of multi-armed bandit problems characterized by monotonic arm weight sequences. This specialized variant has applications in fairness, risk-aware, and personalized online decision-making. Due to the exploration-cost constraint, achieving near-optimal regret for this setting is particularly challenging. Existing algorithms have either focused on a restricted set of monotone sequences or offer high exploration costs. To address this, we introduce a novel bandit selection algorithm that accommodates both non-decreasing and non-increasing arm weight sequences. This algorithm is shown to achieve a regret of $\tilde{O}(T^{1/3}d^{2/3}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i})$, where $\alpha_i$ represents the exploration cost associated with each arm. This near-optimal regret is achieved through a novel approach combining a two-stage exploration strategy and a more efficient arm elimination technique. Specifically, in the first stage, we utilize a near-optimal regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d\sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i})$ by exploring arms using a time- and cost-optimized approach. In the second stage, we eliminate suboptimal arms through a more efficient arm elimination process that achieves a regret of $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{d\sum_{i=1}^d \alpha_i})$. This algorithm is further extended to accommodate non-negative arm weights and achieves a corresponding near-optimal regret. Additionally, we provide lower bounds to demonstrate the optimality of our approach. This research offers the first multi-armed bandit solution capable of handling monotone arm sequences while minimizing exploration costs. Empirical evaluations of our approach verify its performance. Creating original, high-quality art is a highly complex and creative task that people engage in for entertainment and other purposes.  Researchers have been working to develop artificial intelligence systems that can create art by drawing on images, and some have even created original art by combining multiple elements.  However, these systems have limitations in their ability to create original art that is comparable to human-level creativity.  This paper introduces Intelli-Paint, a novel AI system that utilizes a unique approach to generate original art without relying on pre-existing images.  Instead, Intelli-Paint uses a process called "painterly abstraction," where it starts with a detailed image and gradually simplifies it, creating art at each stage.  This approach allows the AI to focus on the fundamental elements of art and replicate human-like painting techniques.  Additionally, Intelli-Paint incorporates a feature that allows it to learn from and be guided by human painters, which enhances its ability to create art that is comparable to human-level creativity.  Experimental results show that Intelli-Paint's unique approach and ability to learn from humans significantly improves the quality of the art it creates, making it a pioneering example of an AI agent that can generate original art that is comparable to human-level creativity.  This breakthrough has the potential to revolutionize the field of computer art and enable AI agents to create high-quality art in the future.  Furthermore, Intelli-Paint's source code has been made available for others to use and build upon.  This advancement holds great promise for future AI research and the potential for AI agents to create art that is comparable to human-level creativity. The findings of the analysis are expected to contribute to the design of advanced wireless communication systems. Random feature maps have been widely used to efficiently learn kernels from large, infinite-dimensional spaces. However, they come with a significant drawback, as the number of features required grows quadratically with the number of training samples. This severely limits their practical applications, especially when dealing with large datasets. This research presents MetaKernel, a kernel learning framework that leverages kernel mean matching to efficiently learn kernel mean maps in these infinite-dimensional spaces. By doing so, it can learn a single feature map that generalizes well to new samples, eliminating the need for additional features. To further optimize performance, MetaKernel incorporates a meta-training procedure that learns feature maps adaptively based on the number of available labels, enabling it to handle small label sets while maintaining competitive results. The proposed framework has been experimentally validated on various real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in achieving state-of-the-art results. Additionally, it has been shown to be particularly effective in small-label settings, where it outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The research also demonstrates that MetaKernel can be effectively integrated with other kernel learning methods, such as kernel ridge regression and support vector machines, to further enhance their performance. This has been experimentally validated on real-world datasets. Given a finite quiver, its double, and a non-abelian gauge theory defined over the quiver double, we establish a correspondence between the quiver representation classification and the reduced phase space of this gauge theory. This reduction is achieved by imposing holomorphic gauge conditions, resulting in a vector bundle known as the reduced bundle, and we prove an isomorphism between the quiver representation space and the global sections of this reduced bundle. Furthermore, by considering quantum observables as correspondences between quiver representations, we demonstrate that quantum quantization and quiver representation quantization are commutative operations. This result is also extended to the case where quiver representations are replaced by quiver algebras and their module categories. Our findings are also applicable in the context of cluster algebras. Finally, we provide a specific example to illustrate these concepts. Our research provides a new method for constructing non-commutative quiver representations, and we discuss potential applications in physics and mathematics, particularly in relation to string theory and the representation theory of quiver algebras. In addition to the core module, we have also developed two specialized extensions, one focused on MCTS-based game agents and the other on adaptive pathfinding agents. We investigate stochastic differential equations with irregular behavior and derive a time-dependent estimate of the distance between their solutions and approximations obtained by averaging over Gaussian distributions under the assumption of locally bounded and time-invariant non-linearity. In cases with smooth non-linearity, this estimate improves with the square of the H\"older constant. Our findings extend existing research by covering equations featuring jump-type noise and providing a uniform bound across time for the distance metric in question. Additionally, we demonstrate that this metric exhibits sublinear growth with respect to the square root of time, contrasting with the geometrically growing distance observed in similar studies. To achieve these results, we introduce novel techniques for analyzing stochastic differential equations with irregular behavior and their approximations. Our approach also includes a new method for approximating the distribution of the stochastic integral of a right-continuous function. In contrast to traditional methods, this approach does not rely on the function's continuity constant. We validate the accuracy of this approximation using a Monte Carlo method. Our work's implications are showcased in the context of stochastic volatility models and risk estimation for complex financial products. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted to verify the theoretical findings. In collaboration with D. Dravelmis, this research is further developed in the study "Risk assessment of complex derivatives in stochastic volatility environments". We present multiple, natural constructions of these sets and establish a broader class of self-similar sets that expand on Bilczok's findings. We are examining a novel approach - utilizing quantum computing for securing Bitcoin transactions - known as quantum bitcoin mining. Our research highlights the scale of the technological hurdles that must be overcome before quantum mining can be integrated into the Bitcoin network, thereby enabling a more sustainable and environmentally-friendly cryptocurrency. This article outlines the process for deriving standardized residuals that are normally distributed and independent, within the context of linear models involving hidden Markov components. Specifically, it addresses the estimation of mean and variance parameters in state transition, measurement, and switching processes, which can be considered standard Gaussian variables. The article provides a closed-form expression for deriving the conditional probability distribution of the hidden state, prior to determining the parameters. The derived formulation of the hidden state transition and measurement functions facilitates the computation of the mean and variance parameters in the observation models. The article further provides a detailed example of applying this method to a linear model featuring a hidden Markov component. The example utilizes a widely-used state-space model to illustrate the practical application of the method. The article concludes by highlighting the broader implications of the derived formulation. The accompanying R code enables readers to easily replicate the results presented in the article. Network security professionals heavily rely on packet capture and network analysis tools to detect and combat malicious threats, but a key challenge arises when dealing with complex, virtualized network infrastructures. Specifically, a common virtualized environment known as Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) often hinders the effectiveness of packet capture by concealing original packet contents. This concealment makes it difficult for standard packet capture methods to function as expected. To address this issue, a team of researchers developed TNT, an innovative network analysis tool that leverages timing information to reveal concealed packet contents. By utilizing precise timing data from network devices, TNT can accurately and efficiently reconstruct original packet contents. Experimental results demonstrate TNT's ability to successfully expose concealed packets with a high degree of accuracy, even when using outdated or compromised timing information. In comparison to existing solutions, TNT offers significantly improved performance and reliability. Additionally, TNT's capabilities are shown to be highly effective in detecting and mitigating malicious threats by identifying malicious packets and preventing the propagation of malicious traffic. Seismic interpretation techniques have been enhanced through machine learning, particularly when dealing with complex, noisy images. However, the development of effective deep learning models is hindered by the challenges of collecting large annotated datasets and training computationally intensive convolutional neural networks. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that utilizes a joint inversion-segmentation model to automate seismic interpretation. This approach is applied to a real dataset consisting of aligned seismic images, allowing the model to be trained on multiple images in a single pass. To evaluate its performance, the joint inversion-segmentation model is compared to a standard segmentation model and a seismic interpreter. Results show that the joint model performs similarly to the interpreter for segmentation, while its joint inference capability enables faster prediction times. Furthermore, the joint model's joint inversion output exhibits a high correlation with the interpreter's results, indicating its potential as a valuable interpretation tool. This work is a pioneering effort in integrating the concepts of machine learning, seismic interpretation, and inversion, with the ultimate goal of reducing the human workload in seismic interpretation and the entire hydrocarbon exploration process. However, current methods often fail to accurately estimate depth when there's occlusion across views due to the mismatch in calculated costs and depths. To address this issue, we propose a novel occlusion-aware cost constructor and a depth estimator that leverages this feature. The proposed method incorporates two key innovations: an occlusion-aware cost constructor that takes into account occlusion when estimating depth and a depth estimator that utilizes this cost in conjunction with a multi-scale cross-correlation to produce an occlusion-aware depth map. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing state-of-the-art methods, both quantitatively and qualitatively. Furthermore, our approach exhibits promising performance on real-world challenging scenarios involving significant occlusions. The accompanying code will be released upon publication. In our investigation, an optical microlaser with delayed feedback is examined using a pulsed excitable system. Through a comprehensive analysis, it is demonstrated that the effect of delay on the phase portrait results in distinct changes to its shape, leading to either merging or splitting of resonance zones in the parameter space. Additionally, it is discovered that the zone boundaries exhibit a butterfly-like pattern, which is a result of a saddle-node-increment process. Furthermore, it is found that the zone boundaries can be effectively controlled by adjusting the pulse period and amplitude of excitation. Our study provides a deeper understanding of the dynamic behavior of pulsed microlasers and highlights the role of delay in controlling their excitable properties. The findings of this research are crucial for the development of precise microlasers with tunable frequency and pulse-width versatility. The presented results are not only applicable to microlasers but can also be extended to other systems with pulsed excitation. Moreover, this research paves the way for the design of excitator-free systems with delayed excitation. The results of this study are also relevant to the control of excitable waves in biological systems and chemical reactions.
